all_users.description: False (default) restricts to the calling user's entries. True returns every user in the company.

tools.name: list_credit_notes
tools.description: List credit notes. Filter by type ("customer" reduces a receivable, "supplier" reduces a payable) and by status. Newest credit_date first. A note with status "applied" has ALREADY been credited against its linked invoice; "approved" means posted to the ledger but not applied to any invoice; "draft" posts nothing. Returns {credit_notes, total, next_offset}: up to limit rows (default 50, max 75); when next_offset is not null, call again with offset=next_offset for the next page. To total a large book without paging, use detail="summary" (count, total_amount, tax_amount and applied_amount over the WHOLE filter set, no rows) and group_by=status|type|party|month (party = the customer or supplier; groups sum to the totals; at most 200 groups, the rest summed in other). A summary takes no offset. CAUTION: a customer note reduces a receivable and a supplier note a payable, so without type (or group_by=type) the summary adds the two together; the reply says so with mixes_types: true. Totals also count draft and cancelled notes, which credited nothing: pass status, or group_by=status, to size what was actually credited.

offset.description: Rows to skip. Pass the previous page's next_offset; omit for the first page.

detail.description: summary = totals (and groups, with group_by) over the whole filter set, no rows. Default standard (rows).

group_by.description: Group the summary by one of: status, type, party, month. Implies detail "summary".

tools.name: get_credit_note
tools.description: Fetch one credit note by id. Use list_credit_notes to find the id.

tools.name: suggest_receipt_matches
tools.description: Scored shortlist of the customer invoices one incoming bank receipt is most likely to settle. READ-ONLY: it proposes and never posts — apply the result with apply_receipt_to_invoice. Scored on the invoice number appearing in the bank narration (exact or fuzzy), how close the amount is to the outstanding balance, how close the dates are, name overlap, and whether the customer opened the invoice in the portal recently. Roughly 100 out of a theoretical 170 is auto-match confidence. Returns AT MOST 5 candidates: rowsTotal is how many invoices were scored and universeTotal how many were considered, so five out of five and five out of fifty can be told apart. Returns nothing at all for a transaction that is money OUT or that does not exist — a receipt is money in. Does NOT cover supplier invoices, purchase orders or journal lines: use get_match_candidates for a bank line that could be any of those. Never paginates: widening a shortlist past five defeats the point of ranking it.

bank_transaction_id.description: The receipt to match, from list_bank_transactions.

tools.name: list_unapplied_receipts
tools.description: Customer receipts that are in the ledger but attached to no invoice — cash sitting on the Accounts Receivable control account that no document knows about. This is the population apply_receipt_to_invoice exists to clear, and the reason aged_debtors can disagree with the control account. A receipt appears here when its amount exceeds the sum of its allocations, so PARTLY applied receipts appear for their remainder. Cancelled receipts are excluded, and a remainder counts when it survives rounding to cents. THIS IS THE SAME DEFINITION reconcile_subledger uses — one query, one threshold, one status filter — so the two tools cannot answer this question with two numbers. They can still differ in one direction and it is meaningful: this tool counts the cash by the DOCUMENT, and reconcile_subledger measures the same receipts against the AR control account, so a receipt whose journal went somewhere else appears here and explains nothing there; reconcile_subledger names that gap as unapplied_cash_off_control_account. totalUnapplied is the sum over every matching receipt, not just this page. Does NOT cover cash credited to the control account by a plain journal with no customer payment record behind it — that is invisible here by construction and is what reconcile_subledger is for. Receipts whose customer row is missing or deleted are reported in excludedRows with their amount, never silently dropped. Paginate with next_cursor; rows come oldest first. IMPORTANT — THIS BALANCE IS STILL GROWING. Allocating a bank line to a customer posts the DR Bank / CR Accounts Receivable journal and creates the receipt, but applies it to no invoice, so every allocation adds to this total and a bulk run adds hundreds. `origins` splits the total by who created it: an mcp: posting stamp PROVES an agent made it, and agentTools names which tool. Everything else with a journal is reported as "not stamped as an agent" rather than as human, because a human stamp proves nothing — createJournalEntry applies it whenever a caller omits the posting meta. Receipts with no journal at all are counted separately again.

as_at.description: Receipts dated on or before this day, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to today.

detail.description: "summary" returns the totals and completeness only, with no rows — use it to see how much unapplied cash there is before deciding to page through it. Default "standard".

tools.name: list_unapplied_payments
tools.description: Supplier payments that are in the ledger but attached to no bill — cash debited to the Accounts Payable control account that no document knows about. Allocating a bank line to a supplier posts the DR Accounts Payable / CR Bank journal and creates the payment, but applies it to no bill, which is what produces these rows. This is the population apply_supplier_payment exists to clear, and the reason aged_creditors can disagree with the control account. A payment appears here when its amount exceeds the sum of its allocations, so PARTLY applied payments appear for their remainder. Cancelled payments are excluded, and so are draft and approved ones: those have no journal behind them, no cash has left the bank and nothing has reached the control account, so listing them would invent a reconciling item. Only processed and reconciled payments are counted. A remainder counts when it survives rounding to cents, so a hundredth of a cent is not reported as a finding and a whole cent is not discarded. THIS IS THE SAME DEFINITION reconcile_subledger uses — one query, one threshold, one status filter — so the two tools cannot answer this question with two numbers. They can still differ in one direction and it is meaningful: this tool counts the cash by the DOCUMENT, and reconcile_subledger measures the same payments against the AP control account, so a payment whose journal went somewhere else appears here and explains nothing there. reconcile_subledger names that gap as unapplied_cash_off_control_account. totalUnapplied is the sum over every matching payment, not just this page. Does NOT cover cash debited to the control account by a plain journal with no supplier payment record behind it — that is invisible here by construction and is what reconcile_subledger is for. Payments whose supplier row is missing or deleted are reported in excludedRows with their amount, never silently dropped. Paginate with next_cursor; rows come oldest first.

as_at.description: Payments dated on or before this day, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to today.

detail.description: "summary" returns the totals and completeness only, with no rows — use it to see how much unapplied cash there is before deciding to page through it. Default "standard".

tools.name: list_supplier_payments
tools.description: Every supplier payment of the connected company, newest first — any status, applied or not — each with payment_amount, allocated_amount (applied to bills) and unapplied_amount. Use it to match payments against another system (a Sage export) or to review a supplier's payments. Filter by supplier_id, status, from_date/to_date and search (payment number, reference or description). totals are over the WHOLE filter, not just the page. Returns {payments, total, totals, next_offset}: up to limit rows (default 50, max 100); call again with offset=next_offset until it is null. Note: only processed and reconciled payments have posted a journal; a draft or approved payment's allocations are planned, not settled. For the unapplied cash that explains aged_creditors vs the control account, use list_unapplied_payments. To size a large payment book without paging, use detail="summary" (count, payment_amount, allocated_amount and unapplied_amount over the WHOLE filter set, no rows) and group_by=supplier|status|month (groups sum to the totals; at most 200 groups, the rest summed in other). A summary takes no offset. Totals also count draft, approved and cancelled payments, which have not (or never) paid anything: pass status, or group_by=status, to size what was actually paid.

from_date.description: Payments dated on or after, YYYY-MM-DD

to_date.description: Payments dated on or before, YYYY-MM-DD

search.description: Matches payment number, reference or description

offset.description: Rows to skip. Pass the previous page's next_offset; omit for the first page.

detail.description: summary = totals (and groups, with group_by) over the whole filter set, no rows. Default standard (rows).

group_by.description: Group the summary by one of: supplier, status, month. Implies detail "summary".

tools.name: find_double_settlements
tools.description: Supplier bills settled more than once. Reports a bill when (a) its live settlements sum to more than its total (over_settled); (b) summed per kind, its contras cover at least half of it AND another kind (card line, payment or credit note) covers at least half too (multiple_sources — the contra-plus-card-line pattern); or (c) its own amount_paid exceeds its total or its settlements by more than a cent (amount_paid_unexplained: paid by a bank match or an import that left no settlement row; cancelled bills excluded). A settlement is a processed/reconciled supplier payment allocated to the bill, or an approved supplier credit note applied to it. Each payment is classified: "contra" (payment_method contra, or its journal credits an account that is neither a bank/cash account nor one holding statement lines — a clearing or loan account), "card_line" (it came from an imported statement line: a bank or paycard line is matched to its journal, or it settles a bank-first provisional), "unclassified" (it credits an account with no subtype and no statement lines), otherwise "payment"; credit notes are "credit_note". Per bill: bill_id, bill_number, supplier, total, amount_paid, settled_total, over_settled_by, reasons, and each settlement (kind, document id + number, date, amount, and — when the token also has read:reports — the account the payment credited). amount_paid is the bill's own column and can differ from settled_total where a bank match or an import set it without a settlement row. Filter by supplier_id and by the bill's invoice date (from / to). Returns {bills, total, next_offset}: up to limit bills (default 50, max 200); call again with offset=next_offset until it is null. At most 50 settlements are listed per bill (settlement_count is the full number). To undo a contra that double-settles a bill, see void_payment.

from.description: Bills dated on or after, YYYY-MM-DD

to.description: Bills dated on or before, YYYY-MM-DD

offset.description: Rows to skip. Pass the previous page's next_offset; omit for the first page.

tools.name: list_fiscal_periods
tools.description: Every fiscal period the company has, oldest first, with its dates and its status (open, closing, closed or locked). This is the posting lock: a journal dated inside an open period posts, and one dated inside a closed or locked period is refused. Two fields exist because the control is commonly inverted and otherwise invisible. open_prior_periods counts periods that have ENDED and are still open — anyone can still post into them, and one production company has 56. alignment compares the period layout against companies.financial_year_start: when aligned is false the periods run January–December while the financial year does not, so a "fiscal year" here is not the year the financial statements cover. financial_years lists the stored financial years with their real dates: after a change of financial year end one of them is a transition year (kind "transition", 1-15 months) and later years run twelve months from its end, so alignment legitimately reflects the NEW start month. The change itself is made in the app (Settings > Change financial year end), not through MCP. It does NOT tell you whether a period SHOULD be closed — call period_close_checklist for that. Read-only. Filter by fiscal_year or status; page with cursor.

cursor.description: next_cursor from the previous page. Loop until it is null.

tools.name: get_fiscal_period
tools.description: One fiscal period by id, with its dates, its status and how many journal entries sit in it. Use it before posting a back-dated journal to check the period is open, and after close_fiscal_period to confirm the status changed. journal_entry_count is the number of entries whose fiscal_period_id is this period — a journal posted with NO period at all is counted nowhere and is invisible to the trial balance, so a count of zero on a period with trading in it is a finding, not a quiet month. Read-only.

tools.name: period_close_checklist
tools.description: Eight readiness checks for one fiscal period, as data: bank reconciled, unposted journals, AR ties to its control account, AP ties to its control account, VAT reviewed, trial balance balanced, opening-balance equity cleared, and journals outside every period. Each returns pass, fail or warn with the reason and the screen that fixes it. orphan_period_journals is the only COMPANY-scoped check: a posted journal with no fiscal period belongs to no period at all, so no period-scoped query can find it, and it is absent from the trial balance, the VAT201 and the AFS while sitting in the ledger. Every close — close_fiscal_period and the app's Close, Bulk Close and Close Year — REFUSES on any failing check, so run this first to see what a close would refuse on. A check that could not be computed comes back as warn with the reason "Could not compute"; close_fiscal_period treats that as a blocker, because "the AP tie could not be checked" is exactly the state in which closing unattended is unsafe. Read-only, writes nothing.

tools.name: bank_statement_coverage
tools.description: Whether a company's imported bank history can account for itself, per bank account. Returns first and last transaction date, transaction count, count and net movement by month, runs of consecutive days with no transaction (day-level gaps), references carried by more than one transaction, the recorded opening balance, and THREE balances kept separate: gl_balance (what the ledger says), statement_balance (what the imported lines sum to) and computed_balance (opening balance plus those lines). gl_vs_computed_difference is the gap between the first and the third — on one production company it is R2.4m and on another R6.5m. They are NEVER netted into one figure: the gap is the finding. Covers every account of subtype bank INCLUDING deactivated ones, because a deactivated account still holds money, and including one whose account_type is not asset: misclassified is true for those, and their gl_balance reads 0 because the cash figure correctly refuses to count a liability as cash, so the whole statement balance shows as unexplained. That is a chart-of-accounts defect to report, not a row to hide. What it cannot do: it cannot see a transaction that was never imported. A gap is evidence that lines are missing; the ABSENCE of a gap is not evidence that they are all there, since a whole month missing from the start or the end of the history leaves no gap between two dates. Use stale_days and the month table against the statements you hold. Read-only. Narrow with bank_account_id (a GL account id from bank_accounts_status).

bank_account_id.description: Optional. A bank GL account id. Omit for every bank account.

as_at.description: YYYY-MM-DD. Everything is bounded at this date. Defaults to today.

min_gap_days.description: Shortest run of empty days worth reporting. Default 7. Weekends make two-day gaps ordinary, so a low value returns noise.

detail.description: summary returns the totals only; standard returns one row per account without the month table; full adds months, gaps and duplicate references.

tools.name: get_opening_balances
tools.description: The opening balance recorded for each bank account, from BOTH places it is stored, so they can be compared. posted_amount is the net of the opening-balance journals actually in the ledger (source auto_migration) and carries the journal ids behind it; metadata_amount is gl_accounts.bank_opening_balance, which the banking screens display and which no balance calculation ever adds. set_opening_balance writes both; the bank-account editor writes only the second, so an account can show a figure on screen that the ledger has never seen. `agrees` is false when they differ by a cent or more, and `disagreements` lists exactly those accounts — that gap is the finding, and the two numbers are never reconciled into one. accounts_without_opening_balance lists accounts with neither: the column DEFAULTS to 0.00 rather than NULL, and set_opening_balance refuses a zero, so a stored zero means unset. Covers deactivated accounts too. Read-only.

bank_account_id.description: Optional. Narrow to one bank GL account.

tools.name: list_employees
tools.description: List payroll employees with their employment status, start and end dates, and whether they are excluded from UIF. Returns EVERY status by default — active, terminated, suspended — because a listing that silently showed only active staff would hide exactly the leaver whose final pay run you are chasing. Pass status to narrow it. SA identity numbers and SARS tax numbers are MASKED to their last four digits unless you pass reveal_identity_numbers: true; they are personal information under POPIA and an agent reconciling headcount does not need them. This is the payroll employee master, NOT the application users returned by company_profile, and NOT the AR customers returned by list_customers. It does not tell you what anyone was paid — that is list_pay_runs for the totals, and the run itself for per-employee lines. Paginated: pass the returned next_cursor to get the following page. rowsTotal is the number matching your filter; a completenessFault means the report could not account for every candidate row and says how many.

reveal_identity_numbers.description: Return full SA ID and tax numbers instead of the last four digits. Personal information — ask only when you need it.

tools.name: get_employee
tools.description: One payroll employee by id. Use after create_employee or update_employee to read the record back, and before assign_employee_component to confirm you have the right person.

tools.name: list_payroll_components
tools.description: The pay components this company can assign to an employee — basic salary, allowances, deductions, employer contributions. Resolve component_id here before calling assign_employee_component. Each carries the SARS source code it reports under and whether it is taxable and subject to UIF and SDL, which is what drives the engines.

tools.name: list_employee_components
tools.description: One employee's pay components, with the assignment_id that end_employee_component takes. An employee with nothing here is paid NOTHING — the run costs earnings from these, so check this before costing a run rather than after wondering why gross is zero. Closed assignments are included: an ended component explains a past run.

tools.name: list_pay_runs
tools.description: List payroll runs with their statutory totals — gross, PAYE, UIF (employee and employer combined), SDL, ETI and net pay — and whether each one actually reached the general ledger. posted_to_gl is the field that matters: a run can be calculated and approved and still have posted NOTHING, which is the state these books were found in. journal_entry_id names the journal when it did post. Filter by year or status. Statuses run draft → calculated → approved → paid; only an approved run can post its journal. It does NOT return per-employee payslip lines, EMP201 totals for a SARS period, or IRP5 data — those are separate calls. The UIF total is the employee and employer halves combined, so an EMP201 needs it split. rowsTotal counts the runs matching your filter and the envelope counts the whole company as its universe, so a status filter that hides 85 of 86 runs shows up as a completenessFault rather than as a short list.

tools.name: emp201_status
tools.description: The SARS EMP201 position for a period: PAYE withheld, the ETI claimed against it, PAYE actually payable after that offset, UIF split into the employee and employer halves, SDL, and the pay runs each figure came from. It counts only runs in a DECLARABLE status — approved or paid. A draft or calculated run is not a finalised payroll and must not be declared, and a cancelled one never counts. It reports the runs it used so you can check that against list_pay_runs; if a month you expected is missing, the run was almost certainly never approved. The UIF split is an approximation. payroll_run_headers stores a single combined employee-plus-employer total, so this halves it. Where the two halves genuinely differ — an employee over the UIF ceiling, or one excluded from UIF — the split will be wrong even though the combined total is right. It also declares SARS tax directives paid OUTSIDE payroll in the period, dated by their posted journal: their PAYE is in paye_withheld and their gross in taxable_remuneration, counted in directive_payments_count and directive_payments_paye. rows are the runs only, so with such payments the rows do not sum to paye_withheld. taxable_remuneration includes non-cash fringe benefits (the low-interest loan benefit, taxed but not paid). A row's gross_pay is cash only, so with such a benefit the rows do not sum to taxable_remuneration either. It does not file anything, does not compute penalties or interest, and does not know what was actually paid over to SARS. It tells you what the payroll says is owed for the period, not what is outstanding.

tools.name: irp5_data
tools.description: Per-employee annual payroll totals for a SARS tax year, as an IRP5 / IT3(a) needs them: cash gross pay, non-cash fringe benefits by SARS code, taxable income, PAYE, the employee and employer UIF halves, SDL, ETI and net pay, with the number of pay runs behind each employee. The SA tax year runs 1 MARCH to 28 or 29 FEBRUARY, so tax_year 2026 means 2025-03-01 to 2026-02-28. Pass the year the tax year ENDS in. It counts only DECLARABLE runs — approved or paid — using the same status list as emp201_status, so a certificate and a monthly declaration cannot disagree about which runs happened. Runs inside the year that were never approved appear in excludedRows as run_not_declarable with the remuneration they carry, because "this employee earned nothing" and "this employee's runs were never approved" are different facts. SA identity numbers and SARS tax numbers are MASKED to their last four digits unless you pass reveal_identity_numbers: true. They are personal information under POPIA. This is the DATA for a certificate, not a certificate. It does not allocate amounts to SARS source codes, does not validate against the IRP5 rules, does not produce an EasyFile export, and does not file anything. gross_salary is CASH pay: a non-cash fringe benefit (the low-interest loan benefit) is not in it but in fringe_benefits, by SARS source code (3801), and is in taxable_income and paye; gross_salary plus fringe_benefits is the remuneration. warnings names each employee whose 3801 items were paid in cash (runs costed before the benefit was non-cash), which are therefore inside gross_salary. cash_allowances lists the travel allowance (3701), which is INSIDE gross_salary but certified under its own code; paye_4582 is the part of 3701 + 3802 that PAYE was withheld on (80% or 20%). Other allowances are not aggregated here.

tax_year.description: The calendar year the SA tax year ENDS in, e.g. 2026 for 2025-03-01 to 2026-02-28.

reveal_identity_numbers.description: Return full SA ID and tax numbers instead of the last four digits. Personal information — ask only when you need it.

tools.name: customer_statement
tools.description: A running-balance statement of account for one customer: every invoice, receipt and credit note dated on or before as_at, in date order, with the balance after each. This is what you send a debtor when you chase them. It runs from INCEPTION to as_at, not over a rolling window — from_date reports the date of the earliest transaction it actually found. Invoices appear at their full value; the statement does not net payments off individual invoices, it lists them as separate credits, so the closing balance is what the customer owes overall rather than an age analysis. Use aged_debtors for ageing. An invoice that is draft, pending approval or cancelled is not yet a claim on the customer and is left off the statement — it appears in excludedRows with its amount and status, never silently. A NULL status counts as issued. A receipt that has not been confirmed or reconciled does NOT reduce the balance and appears in excludedRows with its amount, because a customer who has paid you money nobody has confirmed is a different problem from one who has not paid. Credit notes count whether they are approved or already applied to an invoice. Every excluded row names a machine-stable reason and, where it has one, its amount. detail: "summary" returns the totals with no rows; "standard" and "full" return the transactions. Balances are exact to the cent.

tools.name: project_profitability
tools.description: Per-project profit and loss over a date range, built from posted journal lines tagged with a project: revenue, direct cost, profit and margin for each project, with the account-level lines behind them. basis picks WHICH project: "jobs" (the default) is the job a line carries (project_id, a projects row — what invoices, WIP and time use; project_name is the job name); "cc2" is the CC2 cost-centre dimension (project_id is the CC2 cost-centre id, project_name "<code> — <name>"; for the same split as columns that tie to the statement, use profit_and_loss with group_by cc2). The two are different ids and are never mixed; the coverage is on the same basis. READ THE COVERAGE BEFORE THE ROWS. Only journal lines tagged on the chosen basis can appear here, and an untagged ledger produces an EMPTY result that looks identical to a company with no unprofitable projects. project_tag_coverage reports how many P&L lines in the range are tagged, how many are not, and what the untagged movement is worth. It sits OUTSIDE the completeness envelope on purpose: untagged lines are not projects, so they are a disclosure about data this report could not attribute rather than rows excluded from its universe. On the books this was built against, that total is 100% of P&L. It draws only on the general ledger. Time entries, work items and purchase orders that have never been journalised do not appear, so a project can look costless because nobody posted its costs. It is not a job-cost report and it does not accrue work in progress — see wip_report for unbilled time. as_at is the END of the range. Margin is profit as a percentage of revenue, and is zero when there is no revenue rather than infinite.

basis.description: jobs (default): the job (project_id); cc2: the CC2 cost centre.

tools.name: wip_report
tools.description: Unbilled work in progress for an accounting practice, one row per practice client: total hours, total value at the rate that was applied when the time was logged, and the date of the OLDEST piece of unbilled work — which is the number that tells you where the practice is losing money. It counts APPROVED, billable time that has not yet been billed. It does NOT count time still in draft or submitted, non-billable time, leave, or time already written off or invoiced — so it understates total unbilled effort, and a client with hours sitting in draft shows as having no WIP at all. Use list_time_entries with a status filter to see those. This is practice time, not project costing: it reads the practice time-entry ledger and has nothing to do with journal entries, so nothing here has reached the general ledger. Value is hours times the applied rate and carries no VAT. detail: "full" returns the individual time entries behind each client total, so you can see what the work was. Filter by practice_client_id, partner, or entry-date range.

tools.name: list_fixed_assets
tools.description: List the fixed assets on the register as at a date: asset number, name, category, status, purchase date and price, accumulated depreciation and net book value. An asset DISPOSED on or before as_at is not carrying amount and is excluded from the rows and the totals — it appears in excludedRows as disposed_before_as_at with the book value it was still carrying, because "there is one asset and it was sold" and "there are no assets" are different facts. Assets bought after as_at do not appear at all. This is the SUBLEDGER, not the balance sheet. The figures come from the assets table and are whatever was last written there; they are not derived from journal entries and nothing here proves the ledger agrees. Call asset_register to compare the two — on these books they differ. Depreciation shown is the accounting (policy) figure on the asset record, not the SARS wear-and-tear allowance, and it is only as current as the last depreciation run.

tools.name: asset_register
tools.description: Reconcile the fixed asset register to the general ledger as at a date, and report the gap. This is the assurance call: it returns the register carrying amount, the GL carrying amount, and the difference between them, with the individual GL accounts behind each side. The GL side is selected by account SUBTYPE — fixed_assets for cost, accumulated_depreciation for the contra — never by account name, because choosing a bucket by name is how two default_expense accounts became cost of sales and overstated gross profit by R562,428. It applies NO is_active filter: a deactivated account with a balance is still on the balance sheet. READ THE ACCOUNT LIST, NOT JUST THE TOTAL. On these books every account subtyped fixed_assets that carries a balance is an intercompany loan or investment account, so the total presents millions of rands of loans as property, plant and equipment. The list is what makes that visible. reconciled is true only when the difference is exactly zero. A non-zero difference does not tell you which side is wrong — a register that was never posted to the GL, depreciation journalised against no asset, or an account with the wrong subtype all produce one. It reports the gap; it does not repair it, does not run depreciation, and does not post anything.

tools.name: reconcile_fixed_assets
tools.description: Reconciles the fixed asset register to the general ledger as at a date and DECOMPOSES the difference into itemised reconciling items, each carrying the id of the asset or the GL account behind it. Use it to answer "why does the balance sheet disagree with the asset register", not merely "by how much". asset_register reports the same two totals without the items. Returns registerNetBookValue (cost less accumulated depreciation from the assets table), glNetBookValue (posted balances of every account subtyped fixed_assets or accumulated_depreciation), difference = register less GL, and one row per asset and per account. Each row contributes its own amount to the difference. THE TWO SIDES ARE INDEPENDENTLY DERIVED: the register comes from the assets table and the ledger from posted journal lines, so the difference can genuinely be non-zero. WHAT A ZERO DIFFERENCE DOES AND DOES NOT PROVE. READ THIS BEFORE RELYING ON IT. It is NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT. The items sum to the difference by construction — every asset and every account is reported — so a zero says the two totals happen to agree, NOT that the register and the ledger describe the same assets. Two errors that cancel satisfy it exactly. Treat a zero as an invitation to INSPECT THE ITEMS, never as a conclusion about the accounts. WHAT TO INSPECT. normal_balance_violated marks a cost account carrying a CREDIT balance, or an accumulated-depreciation account carrying a DEBIT one: the sign is opposite to what the subtype implies, so the account is unlikely to be property, plant and equipment. On these books that flag catches millions of rands of loan and investment accounts subtyped fixed_assets, which any single total would present as PPE. The tool REPORTS them; it does not reclassify anything and does not change the chart of accounts. register_linkage_available is false when NO asset and no asset category in the company records a GL account — the state of every production company today. While it is false NO part of the ledger can be attributed to a specific asset, by any means, because the data that would make the link does not exist. Items therefore carry no per-asset attribution field: there is nothing to compute one from, and a field that could only ever hold one value would read as a check that had run. ACCOUNT SELECTION is by SUBTYPE, never by account name — choosing a bucket by name is how two default_expense accounts became cost of sales and overstated gross profit by R562,428. There is NO is_active filter: a deactivated account with a live balance is still on the balance sheet. An asset disposed on or before as_at is not carrying amount; it appears in excludedRows with the book value it was still carrying, never silently dropped — as disposed_before_as_at when a journal posted for it, and as disposal_not_posted_to_ledger when none did. READ unposted_disposals. A disposal the register recorded and the ledger never heard about is the one register-versus-ledger break that can NEVER move the difference: the asset is out of the register carrying amount and the journal is absent from the ledger, so both sides are zero and the arithmetic closes over a real loss. unposted_disposal_gain_loss is profit or loss that never reached the income statement and unposted_disposal_book_value is cost less depreciation never removed from the balance sheet. Production holds exactly one disposal and it is in this list: Brightsphere COMP-0001, sold 2026-04-12 for R8,000 against a R15,000 book value, a R7,000 loss with no journal. disposal_record_count above 1 means the asset carries more than one disposal record: the LATEST is reported, and where an older one posted while the newest did not the amounts shown describe the older event — go and look at that asset rather than trusting the figures on it. It cannot post on ANY tenant — posting a disposal resolves the system account role disposal_profit_loss and no company has an account carrying that subtype, so the posting throws before it writes. Fixing that is a chart-of-accounts change; this tool reports it and changes nothing. READ disclosures BEFORE TRUSTING A ZERO. Accounts are selected by SUBTYPE, so an account typed asset that carries NONE is in neither side of this reconciliation — and because the items and the totals come from the same subtype-filtered query, its balance could never make the difference non-zero. Every such account is listed in disclosures with its id and balance, and unsubtyped_account_balance totals them: Velocity Fibre has 58 holding R32,747,547.38, including PPE cost and accumulated-depreciation accounts. They are DISCLOSURES and not excludedRows on purpose — an exclusion is a row that belonged to this report and was withheld, while these were never in its universe, and most of them are debtors or cash rather than fixed assets. This tool cannot tell which is which, because nothing here is inferred from an account NAME. A difference of zero alongside a non-zero unsubtyped_account_balance is not a reconciliation; set the subtype with update_gl_account and re-run. WHAT CHECKS WHICH NUMBER. difference, itemsTotal and unexplainedDifference are guarded by an arithmetic you can verify: the items sum to the difference. The three figures reported BESIDE them — unsubtyped_account_balance, unposted_disposal_gain_loss and unposted_disposal_book_value — sit outside that identity because the facts they carry genuinely do not belong inside it, and unexplainedDifference of 0.00 tells you NOTHING about whether any of them is right. Each is instead checked against THE ROWS THIS RESPONSE CARRIES, which catches a capped list or a duplicated row, and figure_guards reports the OUTCOME of that check rather than a promise of it: "enumerated" means the comparison ran and agreed, "unguarded" means the rows were not emitted and nothing checked the figure. disclosureFault appears when a check ran and disagreed. NO check can test the query that found the rows, so a disclosure or a disposal the predicate never matched is invisible to every number here. This report makes NO completeness claim (universeTotal is absent) because its rows are PRODUCED by the reconciliation rather than selected from a pool; a universe here could only be synthesized from the numbers it would be checked against, and a claim that cannot fail is worse than none. detail: "summary" returns the totals only, "standard" (default) returns one row per reconciling item, "full" returns one row per journal entry posted to the asset-section accounts — capped at 50 entries per account, most recent first — and is paginated; call again with cursor until next_cursor is null. Follow a journal_entry_id with list_journals or audit_trail, and an asset_id with list_fixed_assets. It reports the gap; it does not repair it, does not run depreciation and posts nothing.

as_at.description: Reporting date, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to today.

detail.description: summary = totals only; standard (default) = reconciling items; full = the journals behind the accounts.

tools.name: run_depreciation
tools.description: Runs the monthly depreciation for every eligible fixed asset in one period, writing the per-asset result to the fixed asset subledger and posting DR Depreciation Expense / CR Accumulated Depreciation to the general ledger. period_date is the LAST DAY of the period being depreciated (YYYY-MM-DD) and defaults to the last day of the current month. It decides the journal date, the journal entry number (DEP-<asset number>-YYYY-MM) and the subledger period, so a run for an earlier month posts into THAT month. ALWAYS CALL IT WITH dry_run: true FIRST. The dry run returns the journals that would post, in full, with the account codes and the amounts on both legs, and the assets that would be skipped with the reason for each. It writes nothing and does not consume the idempotency key. dry_run defaults to FALSE: a call without it POSTS. It refuses BEFORE writing anything when no fiscal period covers period_date, when that period is closed or locked, or when no asset would post. Those are different refusals because the remedies differ — create the fiscal year, re-open the period, or look at why every asset was skipped. An asset is skipped, not failed, when it is not in service (disposed, retired), has no purchase price, is marked below the capitalisation threshold, has no useful life on itself or its category, already has an unreversed journal for this period, or already has a subledger row for it. Re-running a period is therefore safe on both keys — the journal by entry number, and the subledger by asset and period, which is the one that catches an asset whose policy charge is zero and therefore never took an entry number. READ glFailed ON THE REPLY. It counts assets whose subledger row and journal were rolled back together as a unit while the rest of the run committed. A success with glFailed above zero is a PARTIAL run and accumulated depreciation is understated by those assets until the cause is fixed and the period re-run. It depreciates on the ACCOUNTING (IAS 16) policy only in the general ledger; the SARS wear-and-tear figure is computed and stored in the subledger but is not journalised. It does not create assets, does not dispose of them, and does not reclassify any account. Call reconcile_fixed_assets afterwards to check the register against the ledger — on these books they do not agree, and a depreciation run does not make them.

period_date.description: Last day of the period to depreciate, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to the last day of the current month.

dry_run.description: Preview only. Returns the journals that would post, the documents whose balances would change, and the rows that would be skipped — and writes nothing. Run this first on any batch.

idempotency_key.description: Caller-chosen key that makes a retry safe. Reusing a key returns the stored result of the original call instead of writing again. Required on every write.

company_id.description: OPTIONAL guard, not a selector. The connector always acts on the company your token is bound to; passing this asserts which company you BELIEVE that is, and the call is refused if it differs. It can never redirect a write to another company. Resolve it once with list_companies.

tools.name: list_items
tools.description: List the item master — the products and services that can go on an invoice, quote or purchase order: code, description, type, unit, cost price and selling price. This is the `items` catalogue, which is SEPARATE from the `products` table that stock movements are recorded against. It is empty on every company in these books, so an empty result means nothing has been catalogued rather than that the search matched nothing. Use stock_valuation for what is physically on hand. It lists both active and inactive items by default; pass active to narrow. Soft-deleted items never appear. Prices are the catalogue defaults, not what any particular document was actually billed at. Results are capped at 500 rows and there is no cursor — narrow with q or category_id if you hit the cap.

tools.name: stock_valuation
tools.description: Quantity on hand and value per product as at a date, derived from stock movements: inbound movements add, everything else subtracts, and value is the cost recorded ON each movement. READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING THE TOTAL. Every stock movement in these books is a purchase carrying total_cost 0.00, so stock has been received and never valued — the report returns a real quantity against a zero value and flags each such product with unvalued: true rather than presenting R0 as a valuation somebody computed. It reads the products/stock_movements model, which is the one that holds data. The items and stock_items catalogues are separate and empty; list_items shows the first of those. stock_movements and stock_levels have NO company_id column of their own, so this report is tenant-scoped by joining products. Movements whose product carries no company_id belong to no tenant and are NOT attributed to you. Their EXISTENCE is disclosed in excludedRows as product_has_no_company; their number and value are withheld on purpose, because that query cannot be scoped to you and any figure it returned would be computed from rows that may belong to other tenants. Stocktake movements record an absolute quantity rather than a change and are excluded from quantity on hand as stocktake_count_not_a_delta. universeTotal counts YOUR products; neither disclosure inflates it. It is not a stock ledger and does not show individual movements, does not apply FIFO, weighted-average or any other costing method beyond the cost written on each movement, and is not reconciled to any GL inventory account.

tools.name: supplier_statement
tools.description: A running-balance statement of account for one supplier: every bill, payment and supplier credit note dated on or before as_at, in date order, with what we owe after each. The mirror of customer_statement, and it runs the OTHER WAY — a bill credits the balance (we owe more), a payment debits it (we owe less), and a positive closing balance means we owe the supplier. It runs from INCEPTION to as_at, not over a rolling window; from_date reports the date of the earliest transaction it actually found. A bill that is draft, pending approval or cancelled is not yet an obligation and is left off the statement — it appears in excludedRows with its amount and status, never silently. A NULL status counts as issued. A payment that has not been PROCESSED does not reduce what we owe and appears in excludedRows with its amount — there are 56 draft supplier payments on these books, and a payment sitting in draft is a different problem from one that was never raised. Credit notes count whether they are approved or already applied. This is OUR ledger of the supplier. It is not the reconciliation of a statement the supplier sent us — that is supplier_statement_reconciliations in the app, and this tool does not read it. detail: "summary" returns the totals with no rows. Balances are exact to the cent.

tools.name: job_cost_report
tools.description: Logged effort and its value across EVERY time-entry status, grouped by practice client, job category or work item: hours, value and entry count in each status, plus the unbilled total. READ THIS INSTEAD OF wip_report IF YOU WANT TO KNOW WHAT IS OWED. wip_report counts only APPROVED, billable, unbilled time — the correct definition of work in progress and a badly incomplete picture of unbilled effort. On these books it returns 24 entries worth R42,455, while 2,013 entries worth R2,448,850 sit in submitted: logged, sent for approval, and never approved. Showing the statuses side by side is what makes that blockage visible; a WIP figure alone is out by R2.4m. unbilled_value counts billable time at ANY approval status that has not yet been billed or invoiced. Non-billable time and leave are in the status buckets and the totals but never in unbilled_value. Value is the line_total STORED on each entry — hours times the rate that applied when it was logged — not recomputed here, because hours is NUMERIC(6,2) and re-deriving the money reintroduces a rounding difference. It carries no VAT. This is practice time only. Nothing here has reached the general ledger, and it does not include materials, subcontractors or any cost that was journalised — project_profitability covers the GL side. An entry with no client, category or work item cannot be grouped and appears in excludedRows with its value.

tools.name: budget_variance
tools.description: Budget against actual for every revenue and expense account over a date range: the budgeted amount for the months in the range, the posted movement, and the variance between them. READ THE EXCLUSIONS BEFORE THE ROWS. Only accounts that carry a budget appear in rows. A deliberate zero budget is a budget: the account is a row (budgeted: true, budget_amount 0), not an exclusion. An account with real spend and no budget cannot produce a variance, so it appears in excludedRows with reason no_budget_set and its actual value — and on a company where nobody has ever set a budget, rows is EMPTY and looks identical to a company that is perfectly on plan. unbudgeted_movement totals what is sitting outside any budget. The actual is posted journal-line movement per account, signed so revenue and expense are both positive when larger: the same figure the trial balance shows. It is deliberately NOT the income statement, and DO NOT "improve" it into one — no cost-of-sales bucketing, no other-income or finance-cost layer, no tax. incomeStatementService has open defects in exactly the classification layer a variance would inherit, and a variance computed against a net profit already known to be wrong is worse than no variance, because it wears the authority of a reconciliation. The raw per-account aggregate borrows none of it. Draft journals are excluded. Each row carries two signed differences. variance is signed so positive is favourable: revenue actual less budget, expense budget less actual. movement is actual less budget for every account type, the figure the Budget vs Actual screen and CSV print; favourable (true/false) says whether it is good news. variance_pct and movement_pct are percentages of the absolute budget, and variance_pct is null where the budget is zero or absent: there is nothing to be a percentage of. There is no totals field: net profit is sections.net_profit. sections carries revenue, expense and net_profit (revenue less expenses), each with budget, actual, variance, movement, variance_pct, movement_pct and favourable, and they cover EVERY account in the range, budgeted or not: they do not foot to the rows, and excludedRows carry an actual amount, not a variance. Read sections, not a sum of rows, for the whole picture. Budgets are stored per calendar month (budget_month_amounts), not per fiscal year: the budget for a range is the sum of the budgeted months from the month of period_start to the month of period_end, a month counted whole, across as many financial years as the range spans. A financial year can be 1-15 months long (a 14-month transition year after a change of year end), and any window sums exactly its months. fiscal_year is the financial year holding period_start and months_covered lists the YYYY-MM months summed, so the match can be re-derived rather than assumed. detail: "summary" returns sections with no rows; "standard" and "full" return the account lines. VERSION AND DIMENSIONS (optional; with none of them, everything above holds exactly). Without version_id each financial year is read on its primary budget version; version_id reads that version instead (any status), and the whole range must lie in its financial year. cc1_id, cc2_id and bu_id filter by EXPLICIT dimension level, ANDed: an actual counts when its journal line carries that cost centre at that level (cc1_id = CC1, cc2_id = CC2) and that business unit; untagged lines fall outside a filter that names the dimension. A budget counts under a filter when it was set at the filter or below it (a CC2 budget counts under its CC1). A budget set ABOVE the filter (at company level, or at CC1 when filtering by a CC2) is never split or apportioned: it is reported as unallocated_budget (income and expense separately) and its account appears in excludedRows with reason budget_above_filter. With any of these four arguments the range is read in WHOLE MONTHS: a range that cuts a budget month (period_start not the 1st, or period_end not a month end) has no budget at all (splits_budget_month true), and so does one reaching a financial year with no budget (budget_absent_years) or whose budget is all at other members of the filter (budget_outside_filter_years). In all three the actual of every account is in excludedRows with reason budget_absent. An account budgeted for only part of the range is excluded with reason budget_partial. unbudgeted_accounts and unbudgeted_movement count reason no_budget_set only; excludedTotal counts every reason. Those responses add version (id, name, kind, status, isPrimary), dimension_filter, unallocated_budget (with a dimension), budget_absent_years, budget_outside_filter_years and splits_budget_month; a section budget is null where any account under it is above the filter or partial.

version_id.description: A budget version of the range's financial year; default each year's primary.

cc1_id.description: Filter: a CC1 cost centre (explicit level).

cc2_id.description: Filter: a CC2 cost centre (explicit level).

tools.name: list_budget_versions
tools.description: The company's budget versions, newest year first (primary first within a year), optionally of one fiscal_year (the year's label, e.g. 2027): id, year, name, kind (original | reforecast | scenario), status (draft → approved → locked), is_primary (what reports read when no version is named), cells (amount rows held) and total (decimal text: the sum of every amount the version holds, revenue and expense alike, all months and levels: not a profit figure), version_token, who approved / locked / unlocked it and when, and last_edit (the newest audit row: who, when, what). Paged: limit (default 40, max 50), offset; total and next_offset. Read get_budget for the amounts.

tools.name: get_budget
tools.description: One budget version's amounts as the app's budget grid shows them: version_id, or fiscal_year for that year's primary (else newest) version; version null when the year has none. TRAPS FIRST: rows are (account, level, member) with one decimal-text amount per month; an account is budgeted at ONE level per version (company, or cc1, cc2 or bu members); a header account is a row only when it holds its own amounts (a legacy budget, decision 18), otherwise its sub-accounts are; totals are per section and GP/OP/NP per month over the WHOLE version (not the filtered rows), and for a budget holder over their own slices only (they see nothing else); source tells manual (typed) / driver / override / actual (a reforecast's closed months) when not all manual. Filters: accounts (ids or codes), section, level, member, from_month/to_month (YYYY-MM). Paged: limit (default 50, max 80; 20 with include_notes), offset, next_offset. include_notes adds each page account's budget note (notes are per account and year). include_drivers lists up to 50 driver lines (per-head rates only for owners, admins and managers).

tools.name: get_budget_template
tools.description: The budget template of one budget version, the grid the app's Excel download holds, to edit and send back to import_budget_workbook. WORKFLOW: list_budget_versions (pick the version) → get_budget_template → edit the amounts → import_budget_workbook dry_run true (the diff, totals and plan_hash) → import_budget_workbook dry_run false with that plan_hash → get_budget / budget_variance to check; restore_budget_version undoes the import. format json (default): rows of section, account (code, name, id), at a cc1/cc2/bu grain the dimension (code, name, id), months (one decimal-text amount per YYYY-MM month of the year; null = NOT budgeted, "0.00" = budgeted at zero), fy_total and py_actual (prior-year actual, for reference; both ignored on import), and base (the row's months as read, signed: send it back UNCHANGED; it is what the import compares your months with, so a colleague's save after your read is never reverted), plus version_token and the version's section totals per month (for a budget holder, their slices). Paged: limit (default 40, max 50), offset, rows_total, next_offset; send the rows you changed, from any pages, in one import call or several. format xlsx: the same workbook the app downloads, as file_base64 with file_name and signature, for an agent that can open Excel files (most chat agents cannot: use json); refused when its base64 is over 85 KB (a few hundred rows): use json, or fewer members. TRAPS: an account is budgeted at ONE level per version, so a cc1/cc2/bu template offers only accounts budgeted at that level or not at all (decision 4); at a dimension grain the rows are the named members (members: ids), else the members holding amounts or prior-year activity; header accounts appear only when they hold their own amounts. Needs read:reports.

tools.name: get_three_way

Needs the company's balance sheet and cash budget feature. Money is decimal text (balances debit-positive: liabilities and equity negative), months YYYY-MM. version_id, or fiscal_year for that year's primary. include picks sections (default all but lookback); lists over 50 entries are cut, each with <list>_total beside it. tools.name: propose_reclassification
tools.description: Preview moving posted amounts from one GL account to another. Writes NOTHING. HOW A RECLASSIFICATION IS DONE HERE: it posts a NEW journal — a contra on the source account and the same amount re-applied to the target, one pair per source line — and leaves the original posted lines exactly as they are. It never rewrites gl_journal_lines. That is what keeps a trial balance somebody already signed reproducible, keeps the original classification visible to an auditor, and makes the batch undoable through reverse_journal_entry. RETURNS: every journal that would post in full; the profit and loss before and after, each aggregated independently over the ledger rather than one derived from the other; the source and target account movement; gross and net moved, stated separately because an account used for clearing can show R31.6m gross against R659k net and a net-only reading would call that harmless (movement.grossMoved and movement.netMoved are raw DEBIT-POSITIVE ledger movement; account_movement is normal-balance signed, so a credit-side move shows a negative netMoved); every line that would be skipped with a machine-stable reason; and the source journal entry ids behind all of it. READ THE WARNINGS BEFORE ACTING. no_profit_and_loss_effect means every band is identical before and after, so the move changes no reported figure at all and only merges two account names — which is what happens when both accounts already report in the same band (an expense with no subtype and one subtyped default_expense both land in operating expenses). subtype_remedy_available means the source account is simply missing an account_subtype: setting it with update_gl_account achieves the same reporting goal and MOVES NOTHING, whereas this move merges the source account into the target and no report can tell them apart afterwards. On real books most unclassified accounts are correctly named and correctly loaded — they only lack a subtype — and moving them destroys the split between, say, direct material, sub-contractors and wayleave. collapses_named_accounts means the target already carries value from elsewhere. PERIODS: with no posting_date each journal is dated at its own source line, so the period that incurred the cost keeps it and nothing crosses periods — but every line whose own period is CLOSED is skipped (source_period_closed), because a closed period cannot be posted into. Pass posting_date to date the whole batch in an open period instead; nothing is then skipped for a closed source period, and the charge moves between periods. LIMITS: at most 500 source lines per call — narrow with from/to and run several batches rather than have a batch truncate. Draft journals are not candidates; only posted lines are. Lines on a reversed entry, lines an earlier live batch already moved, the contra legs of an earlier reclassification, and the lines of a year's posted closing journal (year_end_close: it is the lock record and no report reads it) are skipped. Post it with post_reclassification_batch.

source_account_id.description: GL account UUID the amounts currently sit on.

target_account_id.description: GL account UUID they should sit on instead. Must differ from the source.

from.description: Only consider source lines whose journal is dated on or after this day (YYYY-MM-DD). Omit for no lower bound. Use from/to to keep a batch under 500 lines.

to.description: Only consider source lines dated on or before this day (YYYY-MM-DD).

posting_date.description: Date EVERY reclassification journal on this one day instead of on its own source line's date. This is how a closed month is corrected from an open one — and it MOVES THE CHARGE BETWEEN PERIODS: the closed month keeps the original classification and this period carries the correction. Omit it and each journal is dated at its source line, which is period-neutral but skips every line whose own period is closed.

tools.name: export_gl_lines
tools.description: The flat general-ledger export for the finance model: ONE ROW PER JOURNAL LINE, every account (both sides of every transaction), in the fixed column order of the ledger brief §4 v1 contract (schema isaflow-gl-lines-1.0). Columns include Line_ID, Txn_ID, Journal_Type, Document_No (with Linked_Document_Count — above 1, the journal has several documents and Document_No/counterparty show the first), Txn_Date, Period, FY and FY_Period_No on the company's own financial year (named by the year it ends: on a March year Mar-2025 = FY26 period 1), signed Amount_Excl_VAT (debit positive, credit negative), VAT_Code, the GL account and its reporting ladder (class, category, statement line/group, cash class, capex/opex), CC1/CC2/BU codes and names with the CC2 parent, counterparty, bank account on cash lines, Payment_Ref, Posting_Status and Period_Locked. VAT is its own row on the VAT control account, so VAT_Amount is 0.00 on every row and Amount_Incl_VAT = Amount_Excl_VAT in v1; every posted Txn_ID sums to zero. summary is the §9 control block — rowCount = rows paging to exhaustion yields, controlTotal = Σ Amount_Excl_VAT over Posted rows (must be 0.00), unbalancedTxnCount (must be 0) — and comes with the FIRST page only (no cursor); later pages return summary null and carry rowsTotal from the first. detail "summary" returns only that. group_by=account|month|source|status (table lines only) adds groups (line_count, total_debit, total_credit, net per group over the same window; they sum to the summary; at most 200 groups, the rest summed in other) and implies detail "summary"; it takes no cursor. A 500-row page passes 90 KB: size the window with group_by first. Page with next_cursor, sending the same date_from, date_to and status (a cursor is refused with any other). Omit dates for full history. status "all" (default) includes Draft and Reversed journals, labelled; "posted" exports only what feeds the statements. table: "accounts" | "cost_centres" | "business_units" | "counterparties" returns that dimension master instead, paged the same way (limit, next_cursor; row_count on every page) — every code a line carries resolves to a row there. "counterparties" (names and VAT numbers) also needs the read:contacts scope. table "ap_open_items" / "ar_open_items": one row per open bill / customer invoice as at today (Doc_Type invoice) plus the unconsumed credit notes (credit_note) and on-account cash (unapplied_payment / unapplied_receipt) as NEGATIVE rows, with Days_Overdue, Age_Bucket (current|30|60|90|120+, the aging's own bucketing), Outstanding, Disputed, CC1/CC2/BU codes (MIXED when the lines differ) and Has_Document; the first page's summary carries controlTotal (Σ Outstanding + Σ Disputed, schema isaflow-open-items-1.1), agedTotal (the aged_creditors / aged_debtors net total, computed through that report's own functions) and difference (an internal consistency check on the same data, 0.00 — not a tie to the GL control account), plus grossTotal, unappliedTotal, disputedTotal (what Outstanding leaves out but is still owed, so it is already inside controlTotal and grossTotal: do not add it to them; Outstanding + Disputed = the document's balance; AR only) and the gross buckets. Credit and cash rows have blank Days_Overdue and Age_Bucket: only invoices are aged. table "bank_accounts" (also needs read:bank-tx): one row per bank / card account with Ledger_Balance (GL, as at today; blank for an account cash.balance does not hold, counted in summary.noLedgerBalanceCount), last statement date and closing balance (possibly on a reconciliation still in progress — later than the last reconciled date), last completed reconciliation, unreconciled and unallocated line counts, last transaction date, Is_Active. These three are as at today: date_from, date_to and status are refused; page with next_cursor, and a cursor is refused once the table has changed. The same files download as CSV from /api/accounting/gl-lines-export, with a browser session or a Personal Access Token holding the same scopes.

Irreversible except by a reversing entry. Requires the write:post permission. Identify each invoice by its invoice_id (from list_customer_invoices or bulk_create_customer_invoices). An invoice that cannot be approved is SKIPPED, not a failure: not found, already approved, cancelled, or dated in a CLOSED fiscal period — each is listed in "skipped" with its reason and the rest of the batch still posts. ALL OR NOTHING for real faults: if an invoice genuinely fails to post, the whole batch is rolled back, nothing is posted, and the error names the element. A repeated invoice_id is REFUSED (not skipped) — each invoice may appear once. Every posting is attributed to the agent and visible in list_agent_postings. tools.name: allocate_bank_transaction
tools.description: Allocate one bank transaction to a GL account (optionally matching a supplier or customer invoice). Identify the transaction by transaction_id OR by bank_reference — the reference printed on the statement — so you can allocate straight from a statement without fetching ids first (optionally narrowed by bank_account_id). POSTS a journal entry. Every allocation is attributed to the agent and can be undone with reverse_bank_allocation. DIRECTION FOLLOWS THE SIGN: a money-out line against a supplier is a payment (DR Accounts Payable / CR Bank) and a money-IN line is a supplier refund (DR Bank / CR Accounts Payable); a money-in line against a customer is a receipt and a money-out line is a customer refund. A REFUND GETS ITS OWN DOCUMENT: a payment record with payment_method "refund" and a NEGATIVE amount, carrying the journal, applied to nothing. It NETS against that contact's other unapplied cash everywhere that is summed — list_unapplied_payments shows it as a negative row, aged_creditors nets it in that supplier's "unapplied" and "net", and the statement carries it as a negative payment. Name no invoice_id for one: applying a negative remainder to an invoice would un-pay it. A refund LARGER than the on-account credit that contact is holding is REFUSED before anything posts — the contact would then owe the company, which is a receivable and belongs on no payable document. An invoice_id whose direction contradicts the line is REFUSED, never guessed. CASH WITH NO invoice_id IS STILL APPLIED: a supplier or customer line that names no invoice settles that contact's OLDEST open documents first, in full until the money runs out and part-paying the one it runs out on, and the reply lists exactly what it closed in "applications" with the remainder in "on_account". Pass auto_apply:"none" to create the payment or receipt and apply none of it. A vat_code of standard is REFUSED on accounts where no supply can arise (salaries and statutory deductions, taxes and penalties, distributions, depreciation, donations, and exempt financial services such as interest, loans and share investments) and on entertainment accounts where input tax is denied — the line still posts, gross, and the response carries vat_coerced saying what was changed and why. To allocate many transactions at once, use bulk_allocate_bank_transactions.

transaction_id.description: Bank transaction UUID. Supply this OR bank_reference, not both.

bank_reference.description: The reference printed on the bank statement, matched exactly (after trimming) against either reference column on the transaction — the same value list_bank_transactions returns as bank_reference. Use it instead of transaction_id when working from a statement — no id lookup needed. Must resolve to exactly one transaction; if it does not, the tool lists the candidates.

bank_account_id.description: Optional: narrows a bank_reference lookup to one bank account.

contra_account_id.description: GL account UUID the other side of the transaction is booked to. Required for alloc_type "account" (the default); ignored for supplier/customer, which post to the AP/AR control account.

cc1.description: Optional CC1 = FNO / client (code, UUID or alias). Usually omit it: a CC2 derives its FNO, and naming a CC1 that disagrees is refused.

cc2.description: Optional CC2 = project (code, UUID or alias, e.g. "Ben Farms"). Sets the FNO through its parent. A cost-of-sales line without one is reported in dimension_warnings.

bu.description: Optional business unit = function (code, UUID), e.g. "MAINT".

auto_apply.description: What to do with a supplier or customer line that names no invoice_id. "fifo" (the default) applies the cash to that contact's OLDEST open documents, settling each in full until it runs out and part-paying the one it runs out on; the remainder stays on account. "none" creates the payment or receipt and applies none of it, leaving it for apply_supplier_payment or apply_customer_receipt. Ignored on a GL-account line, which settles no document.

company_id.description: OPTIONAL guard, not a selector. The connector always acts on the company your token is bound to; passing this asserts which company you BELIEVE that is, and the call is refused if it differs. It can never redirect a write to another company. Resolve it once with list_companies.

tools.name: reverse_bank_allocation
tools.description: Undo an allocation: reverses the posted journal and returns the bank transaction to unallocated. Identify the transaction by transaction_id OR by bank_reference — the reference printed on the statement — optionally narrowed by bank_account_id. Use to correct a wrong allocation — the original and its reversal both remain in the audit trail. By default the reversing journal carries the ORIGINAL entry's date when that period is still open, and today when it is closed; pass reversal_date to choose it explicitly. The reply carries original_entry_date, reversal_entry_date and date_moved: date_moved true means the correction is NOT in the period it corrects. Reversing a customer receipt whose unapplied cash a customer refund has already returned is refused (reverse the refund first). To undo a whole bulk allocation, use reverse_bank_allocation_batch.

tools.name: reallocate_bank_transaction
tools.description: Re-point a RECONCILED bank line (one in a COMPLETED bank reconciliation) to a different allocation target WITHOUT reopening the reconciliation: the old allocation journal is reversed and a new one posted, BOTH on the ORIGINAL entry date, and the line stays reconciled on the same reconciliation with the same bank side and its reviewer kept — so the reconciliation and the bank balance as at every date are unchanged. target names exactly one of gl_account_id, supplier_id or customer_id. A supplier or customer target creates the payment / receipt / refund allocate_bank_transaction would (auto_apply "fifo", the default, settles the contact's oldest open documents); the old one is cancelled and the bills/invoices it paid reopen. expected_journal_entry_id is the journal the line is reconciled to now (matchedJournalEntryId on a full list_bank_transactions row): a stale one is refused, naming the current one. REFUSED, nothing written: a line that is not reconciled (use reverse_bank_allocation then allocate_bank_transaction), one in an in-progress session or reconciled in the Sage import, a closed or locked fiscal period or a VAT-locked period on that date (the date is never moved), transfers, splits, payment batches, provisional lines, matched (not allocated) lines, journals with reversal history, an invoice target, a bank account as target, and a customer receipt whose on-account remainder a refund has already paid out (re-pointed to the SAME customer, judged on what the new receipt keeps after its auto_apply: refused only if a refund is left uncovered). The same target, VAT code and dimensions (and, for a contact, the same outcome of auto_apply) answers nothing_changed. On a gl_account_id target, omitting vat_type means NO VAT, as allocate_bank_transaction does — send vat_type to keep a VAT claim. A vat_type of standard on an account where no supply can arise is coerced as allocate does and reported in vat_coerced. dry_run is required: true runs the whole reallocation and rolls it back — every id it returns (journals, lines, payment) is rolled back and does not exist afterwards; false does it.

A company that is not VAT registered takes no VAT number or category (register it in Settings first). A value cannot be cleared here. Owner or admin only; acts on the company your token is bound to. CHANGING THE CATEGORY MOVES VAT PERIOD BOUNDARIES: if the company already has VAT returns, VAT period locks (even unlocked ones) or VAT201 versions or a submitted legacy VAT201, the call is refused until you send acknowledge_period_change: true — filed periods are not re-cut and cannot be restored by changing the category back. dry_run is required: true runs every check and the write and rolls it back, returning before/after, the current and next VAT periods under the old and new cycle (period_impact) and the returns on file; false changes it. The reply carries before and after and undo_arguments (the before value of each changed field; calling again with them puts it back) and undo_limitations: a number that was EMPTY before cannot be emptied again, so it has no undo entry. A real change writes an audit_log row.

tools.name: bulk_allocate_bank_transactions
tools.description: Allocate up to 500 bank transactions in one call, each to a GL account (optionally matching a supplier or customer invoice). Identify each transaction by transaction_id OR by bank_reference — the reference printed on the statement. POSTS a journal entry per line. Transactions that are already allocated (or excluded, or otherwise not importable) are SKIPPED, not failures: they are listed in "skipped" with a reason and the rest of the batch still posts, so you can re-send a list without checking it first. A R0.00 transaction (a waived fee, a memo line) has no journal to post and is SKIPPED with reason "zero_amount": it stays imported, and it never rolls the batch back. A transaction_id or bank_reference that matches no transaction — or matches several — is also SKIPPED with a reason, so one unrecognised reference never costs you the rest of the batch. DIRECTION FOLLOWS THE SIGN: a money-out line against a supplier is a payment (DR Accounts Payable / CR Bank) and a money-IN line is a supplier refund (DR Bank / CR Accounts Payable); a money-in line against a customer is a receipt and a money-out line is a customer refund. A REFUND GETS ITS OWN DOCUMENT: a payment record with payment_method "refund" and a NEGATIVE amount, carrying the journal, applied to nothing. It NETS against that contact's other unapplied cash everywhere that is summed — list_unapplied_payments shows it as a negative row, aged_creditors nets it in that supplier's "unapplied" and "net", and the statement carries it as a negative payment. Name no invoice_id for one: applying a negative remainder to an invoice would un-pay it. A refund LARGER than the on-account credit that contact is holding is REFUSED before anything posts — the contact would then owe the company, which is a receivable and belongs on no payable document. A line whose invoice_id contradicts its direction is SKIPPED with that reason, never guessed. CASH WITH NO invoice_id IS STILL APPLIED: each supplier or customer line settles that contact's OLDEST open documents first, part-paying the one the money runs out on, and every line reports what it closed in "applications" with the remainder in "on_account". Lines are applied IN ORDER, so two lines against one supplier consume the same bills in turn. Pass auto_apply:"none" — per line, or once for the whole batch — to create the payments and receipts without applying them. ALL OR NOTHING for real faults: if a line genuinely fails, the whole batch is rolled back, nothing is posted, and the error names the line. Every line is attributed to the agent, and the returned batch_id undoes the posted set through reverse_bank_allocation_batch. Use dry_run to see what would post and what would be skipped; the dry run reports the same zero_amount skips as the live call.

allocations.description: The lines to allocate — at most 500. Each names one transaction and how to book it.

transaction_id.description: Bank transaction UUID. Supply this OR bank_reference, not both.

bank_reference.description: The reference printed on the bank statement, matched exactly (after trimming) against either reference column on the transaction — the same value list_bank_transactions returns as bank_reference. Use it instead of transaction_id when working from a statement — no id lookup needed. Must resolve to exactly one transaction; if it does not, the tool lists the candidates.

auto_apply.description: What to do with a supplier or customer line that names no invoice_id. "none" creates the payment or receipt and applies none of it, leaving it for apply_supplier_payment or apply_customer_receipt. Ignored on a GL-account line, which settles no document.

The default for every line that does not carry its own auto_apply. "fifo" (the default) applies each supplier or customer line to that contact's oldest open documents; "none" leaves the cash on account.

tools.name: auto_apply_unapplied
tools.description: Apply the BACKLOG of unapplied supplier payments, customer receipts and credit notes to the documents they settle: each contact's oldest open documents first, part-paying the one the money runs out on, oldest cash first so a later payment sees what an earlier one consumed. POSTS NO JOURNAL and creates no document — the cash is already in the ledger, and only the subledger moves. Cash is never applied across contacts, and whatever is left over stays on the payment as on-account credit. DRY RUN IS THE DEFAULT: without dry_run:false it writes nothing and returns the full plan, and the plan a dry run returns is EXACTLY what a live run does. Read three lists, not one. "applications" is what would settle; "no_open_documents" is the payments with nothing open to apply to, usually the larger half of the backlog and the part a human has to look at; "skipped" is what the tool may not touch and why — a journal in no fiscal period, a contact that no longer resolves, a draft receipt with no journal behind it. totals.population_amount is every remainder read, and applied + left_on_account + no_open_documents_amount + skipped_amount adds up to it. A live run applies each payment in its own savepoint, so a failure on one is reported in "failed" and the rest still apply. Re-running is safe: an applied payment has no remainder left and is not in the population, so a second run reports 0. Every application is an ordinary allocation row, so void_payment / void_receipt / cancel_credit_note reverse it. Scope it with entity_id to one supplier or customer, and limit to cap how many payments one call walks.

entity_id.description: One supplier (ap) or customer (ar). Omit for the whole subledger.
